docs.text:
ORBIS SMARTFACTORY · MASTER THESIS Camera-based Track & Trace reconstruction

A clear record of the work to follow the FTS and its workpieces from shopfloor video, with optional NFC support.

docs.title: What is being done?
docs.text: The project is bringing FTS tracking, workpiece tracking, recorded replay and NFC input into one understandable demonstration. Each part is kept traceable so that a working demonstration is not confused with a proven scientific result.

docs.title: What is the goal?
docs.text:
The goal is a trustworthy camera-based history of where the FTS and its workpieces moved. NFC may provide a physical identity when vision alone cannot distinguish similar workpieces.

FTS TRACKING Available

The live camera and recorded-session replay can follow the carrier.

NFC INPUT Listening

The dashboard can receive completed NFC reads from the shopfloor broker.

WORKPIECE TRANSFER Blocked

The latest model did not remain reliable under the new camera conditions.

docs.title: What has been implemented?
docs.text:
• Live FTS detection and tracking from the shopfloor camera.
  • Recorded replay with synchronized FTS and exploratory workpiece overlays.
  • A read-only MQTT connection that can receive completed NFC reads; a fresh physical association is still unverified.
  • Prospective workpiece annotations checked by the same reviewer and a provisional evaluation of sealed predictions.
  • A private research website linking the journal, decisions and experiment evidence.

docs.title: What are the consequences?
docs.text:
The FTS path is suitable for continued live testing. The workpiece path is not ready for deployment: model v0.2 performed poorly on the newly recorded scenes. An earlier two-piece feasibility test was promising, but it used a different detector and remains development evidence rather than proof of general use.

Current scientific boundary

The combined replay is an exploratory demonstration. It is not production certification, and the prospective evaluation frames must not be used to tune the next workpiece model.

docs.title: What are the next steps?
docs.text:
1. Restore and verify the exact detector and tracker pair used in the promising two-piece development test.
  2. Connect that workpiece pipeline to the live camera beside the FTS tracker.
  3. Run one synchronized physical test with camera, FTS, workpieces and NFC.
  4. Use a new unseen recording for any later generalization claim.

docs.title: Project path
docs.text:
1. Establish FTS tracking.
  2. Investigate workpiece tracking feasibility.
  3. Evaluate performance on new recordings.
  4. Integrate the demonstration without claiming general reliability.
  5. Conduct a synchronized physical test.

docs.title: Supervisor Briefing
docs.text:
Current status: 15 September 2026

This page gives a short overview of the latest work, its meaning and the next decisions. Detailed technical evidence remains available elsewhere in the research portal.

docs.title: What was the goal?
docs.text: Extend FTS tracking, which works in the observed demonstration, toward workpiece tracking and optional NFC identification, while keeping scientific evaluation separate from the live demonstration.

docs.title: What was done?
docs.text:
• The prospective workpiece annotations were completed and structurally checked; replacement frames received a visual check by the same reviewer.
  • The workpiece model was evaluated on newly recorded shopfloor videos under a declared single-reviewer deviation; results remain provisional.
  • Live FTS tracking, recorded replay and the dashboard were brought together in a separate live-test branch.
  • The dashboard was connected to the shopfloor MQTT broker and can receive completed NFC reads. Association of a fresh physical scan with the correct visible workpiece has not yet been demonstrated.

docs.title: Tools and their role
docs.text: Tool What it does now What comes next Shopfloor camera Provides the live view used to observe the FTS. Capture a synchronized test with FTS, workpieces and NFC. FTS detector and tracker Finds the FTS and follows its movement in the demonstration. Keep this foundation, with its documented limits, for workpiece association tests. Workpiece detector and tracker Tests whether coloured workpieces can be found and followed. Verify the promising two-piece development setup and connect it to live video. MQTT and NFC Can receive the physical NFC identity reported by the shopfloor. Verify that a fresh NFC read is linked to the correct visible workpiece. Dashboard Presents the live camera, recorded replay and system status. Show FTS, workpiece and NFC information together, distinguishing their validation status. Research journal Explains the work, decisions, results and limitations. Continue with short supervisor summaries and separate technical evidence.

docs.title: What did we learn?
docs.text:
The live FTS path works in the demonstration; this does not establish reliability under all conditions. The latest workpiece model performed well on familiar development material but performed poorly under the changed conditions in the new recordings.

An earlier two-piece tracking experiment was promising, but it used a different detector and is development evidence. It must be restored exactly before it can be used as the baseline for the next live test. The development tracker comparison does not establish reliable tracking of two workpieces simultaneously on the carrier.

docs.title: What are the consequences?
docs.text:
• FTS tracking can continue in the live demonstrator.
  • The current workpiece result is not ready for deployment or a general success claim.
  • The combined workpiece replay remains exploratory.
  • The evaluated recordings must not be reused to tune the next model.

docs.title: What happens next?
docs.text:
1. Restore and verify the exact detector and tracker pair from the promising two-piece development test.
  2. Connect this pair to the live camera beside the FTS tracker.
  3. Run one synchronized test with camera, FTS, workpieces and NFC.
  4. Record a new unseen video before evaluating another improved workpiece model.

docs.title: Points for supervision
docs.text:
• Confirm the workpiece baseline to carry into the next live test.
  • Arrange the independent annotation review required for final protocol-compliant evaluation; it has not yet taken place.
  • Agree on the conditions and acceptance criteria for the next unseen recording.

Reading the rest of the portal

The journal explains the work by date. The experiment and decision sections contain the supporting technical record and are not required for this briefing.

docs.title: Evidence-based conclusions
docs.text:
• The 99.8–100.0% output continuity did not represent reliable FTS tracking.
  • The dominant failure is a persistent lock onto a fixed station: 82 reviewed candidates were classified as station_false_lock.
  • Both blue sessions and od_white_1 had zero correct periodic detector locks.
  • Confidence does not separate correct and false locks: mean confidence was higher for station false locks than for correct locks.
  • A detector error can initialize CSRT on the wrong stationary target and still produce an apparently continuous trajectory.
  • The current one-reference YOLOE configuration must not be transferred to live tracking unchanged.

docs.title: Next engineering step
docs.text: Build the verified one-class fts dataset from all six recordings, including negative station-only frames. Then compare improved multi-view YOLOE prompting against a small dedicated detector on held-out videos.

docs.title: Interpretation limit
docs.text: Detector-lock correct rate is checkpoint correctness, not precision or recall. The queue covers periodic detector locks, flagged jumps, and no-output gaps; it does not provide frame-by-frame ground-truth boxes or exhaustive CSRT review.

docs.title: Automated findings
docs.text:
• All six recordings completed and produced FTS position rows plus detector checkpoints.
  • Output continuity is between 99.8% and 100.0% on every recording.
  • CSRT reported zero explicit tracker losses, but this does not prove that it followed the correct object.
  • Four suspicious high-speed jumps require visual review: two in od_blue_1 and two in od_white_2.
  • Mean YOLOE lock confidence is low (0.114–0.136), so false station/object locks remain plausible.
  • The od_blue_2 wall-clock runtime includes several hours while the computer was sleeping. Its 0.51 effective FPS is therefore invalid as a performance benchmark. The other five runs measured approximately 14–23 effective source FPS.
  • 220 detector checkpoint images were saved across the six recordings.

docs.title: Interpretation limit
docs.text: High output coverage only means that YOLOE initialized a box and CSRT continued emitting a box. A tracker can continuously follow the wrong object. Detection recall and exhaustive drift duration cannot be reported without frame-level ground-truth FTS boxes. The completed candidate review below provides checkpoint correctness and classified evidence for the queued anomalies only.

docs.title: Completed manual review
docs.text:
Manual review was completed on 2026-07-28 for all 130 queued candidates. The append-only log contains 304 rows because corrected and repeated saves are preserved; only the latest row for each candidate is used in the statistics.

Session Reviewed candidates Correct detector locks Correct-lock rate Dominant finding od_red_1 13/13 12/13 92.3% Mostly correct; one oversized/wrong box od_red_2 17/17 15/17 88.2% One station lock and one oversized/wrong box od_blue_1 32/32 0/29 0.0% Persistent charger/station lock od_blue_2 31/31 0/30 0.0% Persistent charger/station lock od_white_1 22/22 0/21 0.0% Persistent charger/station lock od_white_2 15/15 10/13 76.9% Mostly correct, with wrong/oversized boxes

Across the 123 periodic YOLOE locks, 37 (30.1%) were judged correct. Across all candidate types, the latest verdict totals are 38 correct FTS, 82 station false locks, 8 wrong objects, and 2 tracker-drift observations. The dominant failure is therefore detector initialization on a fixed station, after which CSRT can continue emitting a plausible but incorrect trajectory.

The confidence score cannot reject these failures: mean confidence was 0.1205 for correct locks and 0.1354 for station false locks. The current single visual prompt and confidence threshold must not be transferred to live tracking unchanged.

See REVIEW_SUMMARY.md and review_summary.json for the reproducible report. Regenerate both with python -m scripts.summarize_fts_review.

The 30.1% figure is checkpoint correctness, not precision or recall. The queue reviewed periodic detector locks, automated jumps, and no-output gaps; it did not create frame-by-frame ground-truth boxes or exhaustively inspect every CSRT frame. Those measurements require the verified dataset in the next milestone.

docs.title: Work completed
docs.text:
• Completed the structured manual review of all baseline candidates.
  • Verified that 130 of 130 unique candidates have a final decision.
  • Generated machine-readable and human-readable review summaries.
  • Added a regression test for latest-decision semantics.
  • Prevented unchanged review decisions from being saved repeatedly.
  • Updated the FTS roadmap: candidate-level baseline complete; ground-truth dataset active.
  • Established the scientific journal, decision register, lesson register, experiment register, and reconstructed project history.
  • Defined the one-class FTS annotation protocol for positive, negative, occluded, ambiguous, and rejected frames.
  • Extracted the deterministic fts-pilot-v0.1 dataset: 48 pending frames from all six recordings, with source-video splits, timestamps, checksums, and six contact sheets.
  • Added an FTS ground-truth annotation workspace to the dashboard. It displays each pilot image, supports mouse-drawn boxes and No FTS/Unsure decisions, and saves YOLO labels plus an append-only decision history without modifying the original image.

docs.title: Method and rationale
docs.text: The append-only review log was not modified or compacted. The latest decision for each (session, candidate) pair was used because this preserves the audit trail while allowing corrections. The review queue included periodic detector locks and automatically flagged anomalies. It was used to test semantic checkpoint correctness, not to estimate frame-level precision or recall.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Review completion: 130/130 unique candidates.
  • Periodic detector locks judged correct: 37/123 (30.1%).
  • Latest verdicts across all candidates:
  • correct FTS: 38;
  • station false lock: 82;
  • wrong object: 8; and
  • tracker drift: 2.
  • Correct periodic detector locks:
  • od_red_1: 12/13;
  • od_red_2: 15/17;
  • od_blue_1: 0/29;
  • od_blue_2: 0/30;
  • od_white_1: 0/21; and
  • od_white_2: 10/13.
  • Mean detector confidence was 0.1205 for correct locks and 0.1354 for station false locks.

docs.title: Mistakes and diagnosis
docs.text:
1. Near-complete output coverage had initially looked like stable tracking. Human review showed that CSRT often tracked a station continuously.
  2. A higher confidence threshold was considered as a simple correction, but the score distributions contradicted it because false locks were more confident on average.
  3. The append-only review contained repeated saves. The records were valid, but the interface did not clearly prevent an unchanged submission.

docs.title: Corrections
docs.text:
• Reported the result as checkpoint correctness rather than precision or recall.
  • Rejected unchanged live transfer of the single-reference YOLOE configuration.
  • Added disabled-state feedback for unchanged review decisions.
  • Defined verified ground truth as the next prerequisite before detector tuning.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Ruff formatting and linting passed.
  • Full test suite passed before journal automation: 30 tests. After adding and validating the journal updater and its regression coverage, the full suite passed with 34 tests.
  • Editor diagnostics reported no errors in changed report, test, JavaScript, and documentation files.
  • Browser validation confirmed that an unchanged decision is disabled and a changed note enables “Save corrected decision” without submitting a new row.
  • Review report regeneration confirmed 130/130 candidates and 37/123 correct detector locks.

docs.title: Interpretation and limitations
docs.text: The baseline cannot be called 30.1% precise or 30.1% accurate over all frames. The reviewed sample was a queue of detector checkpoints and flagged anomalies, not exhaustive frame-level ground truth. The evidence is sufficient to reject the current method for unchanged live use, but not to compare final detector precision and recall.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Manually classify and annotate all 48 pilot frames using the new protocol. Complete a second review of validation and test items, then add targeted frames for any missing empty-scene, strong-motion-blur, difficult-lighting, or occlusion conditions before freezing fts-ground-truth-v1.

docs.title: Method and rationale
docs.text: A five-frame calibration pilot was chosen instead of proposing boxes for all 48 frames. The frames cover different recordings, splits, occlusion conditions, image-edge placement, and blurred poses. A separate proposal file and orange overlay make the machine suggestion visible while preserving explicit human authority. Automatic label creation was rejected because it would contaminate the evaluation set and hide proposal errors.

docs.title: Results and evidence
docs.text:
• Five proposals are stored in data/annotations/fts-pilot-v0.1/ai_proposals.jsonl.
  • Dashboard project state reported 0/48 completed before human review; proposal display does not change that count.
  • Browser inspection confirmed the first proposal rendered in orange and Accept converted it to cyan locally without changing completion progress.
  • Final validation after the immutable-provenance changes passed Ruff, browser JavaScript syntax checking, all 51 tests, and a strict MkDocs build.

docs.title: Problems, mistakes, and diagnosis
docs.text:
Ordinary Next navigation stepped through all 48 frames, making the five proposals hard to review consecutively. A direct Next AI proposal action was added. The box coordinates were estimated from visual inspection and remain uncertain until the human reviewer checks each image; two diagonal-pose images appeared similar and require independent review.

The candidate project initially exposed a validation/test second-review button while all 12 first-pass decisions were still pending. The API rejected an individual unannotated frame, but the browser affordance was misleading. The project-level gate now requires the complete first pass. Manifest selection notes were also hidden and would have been overwritten by an annotator note; they are now preserved as source_notes and displayed as read-only evidence.

docs.title: Corrections or decisions
docs.text: AI proposals remain read-only evidence until explicit human Save. Orange means unverified proposal and cyan means human-selected geometry. Proposal provenance is retained in the decision record, and direct proposal navigation avoids mistaking pending non-proposal frames for completed pilot review.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The five corrected proposals do not establish annotation accuracy, detector precision, recall, frame-level performance, or the usefulness of AI assistance. No proposal was accepted unchanged, so the initial proposal method should not be scaled to the remaining frames without improvement.

The completed annotation pool now contains 60 positives and no full-frame negative. Fixed stations are still present as unlabeled background inside the positive images, but this does not satisfy the explicit empty-label coverage requirement. Continuing to mine the same route recordings is not justified by the failed candidate result; an empty-shopfloor source clip is required.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Capture a short same-camera empty-shopfloor recording with the FTS physically outside the field of view and manually verify its station-dominated and open-floor frames before freezing the combined dataset.

docs.title: Method and rationale
docs.text:
Complete recordings, rather than individual frames, were assigned to one split. The cluttered source belongs to training because it can teach rejection of plausible and artificial confusers. The clean source is held out for test because it answers the primary question: can a detector reject the normal shopfloor when the FTS is absent? Filenames and recording intent were not treated as labels.

The wide-plan source was excluded from the calibrated core dataset because the camera framing differs visibly. Mixing it into the same evaluation would combine object-recognition performance with camera-geometry shift.

docs.title: Results and evidence

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Correct Live FTS visibility and station-transition semantics without changing the frozen detector, selected CSRT tracker, or evidence-based model settings. The operational question was whether temporary visual loss and movement inside a station could be prevented from creating false physical departures.

docs.title: Work completed
docs.text:
• Added a one-second detector-confirmation expiry to remove stale CSRT boxes after the physical FTS leaves the camera view.
  • Published explicit LOST observations instead of extending a visual prediction indefinitely.
  • Separated visual tracking state from business station occupancy: LOST means unknown visual evidence, not physical departure.
  • Changed departure inference to require sustained detected observations outside the station service envelope.
  • Preserved one visit while the FTS moves inside a station or disappears briefly and is reacquired at the same station.
  • Preserved separate visits when a positively observed exit is followed by a return to the same station.
  • Corrected the CHRG service polygon so the observed parked position lies within the calibrated service area.
  • Added regression coverage for temporary loss, same-station reacquisition, in-station movement, true exit and return, and one noisy outside point followed by loss.

docs.title: Method and rationale
docs.text: Two state layers were made explicit. The visual layer reports whether the FTS is currently detected or temporarily predicted. The station layer represents a physical visit and therefore changes only when supported by spatial evidence. This was selected over a fixed grace period because elapsed time cannot distinguish occlusion from physical movement. A departure now requires detected outside observations spanning the configured confirmation interval. The frozen detector, tracker, confidence thresholds, and one-second visual timeout were not retuned.

docs.title: Results and evidence
docs.text:
• Commit eecf202 records 514 additions and 33 deletions across 13 files.
  • The complete automated suite passed: 126 tests.
  • Regression tests demonstrate that temporary LOST plus same-station reacquisition remains one visit.
  • A single detected point outside the envelope followed by LOST does not create DEPARTED.
  • Sustained detected movement outside the envelope still creates DEPARTED, and a later same-station return creates a new ARRIVED visit.
  • CHRG, Live tracking, zone geometry, dashboard contracts, and tracker-adapter behavior are covered by focused tests.

These are deterministic software observations. They support correctness of the implemented state rules for the tested trajectories; they are not a substitute for a new physical all-station route.

docs.title: Problems, mistakes, and diagnosis
docs.text:
• CSRT continued drawing a predicted FTS after physical removal. The root cause was visual prediction state with no detector-confirmation expiry.
  • Movement while docked was interpreted as leaving because occupancy had been coupled to low motion. Low motion is suitable as arrival evidence but not as a continuing-occupancy requirement.
  • Temporary detector loss fragmented a CHRG visit because missing visual evidence had been treated as negative physical evidence.
  • An earlier spatial-exit fallback could convert one noisy outside coordinate plus elapsed LOST time into a departure. The fallback was inconsistent with the requirement for sustained positive evidence.
  • The original CHRG polygon did not include the observed parked center.

docs.title: Corrections or decisions
docs.text:
• Visual presence and station occupancy remain separate state variables.
  • Arrival requires station-local low-motion evidence; continued occupancy does not require continued stillness.
  • Departure requires positive, sustained, detected spatial exit evidence.
  • Temporary LOST never proves physical departure.
  • The frozen model and tracker settings remain unchanged; the corrections are interpretation and state-lifecycle fixes.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The operator was no longer in the test room, so no structured physical route was executed after these corrections.
  • Automated trajectories cannot establish performance under new occlusions, lighting changes, camera displacement, or network interruptions.
  • The CHRG polygon correction is specific to the current 1920×1080 camera geometry and is not an operator-facing recalibration procedure.

docs.title: Supervisor meeting
docs.text: Today I met my company supervisor at ORBIS. I presented the intake connection, the NFC information received through MQTT, and the interface I developed to show the live state. He told me that my journal contained too much AI-generated information. He wants a shorter account in my own words, explaining what I chose to do and why I followed that path from the beginning of the project until now.

docs.title: How I chose the project path
docs.text:
At the beginning, I wanted to make the complete Track & Trace idea visible as quickly as possible. I chose a camera-based system that only observes the shopfloor and does not control it. For the first prototype, I used YOLOE to find the FTS and CSRT to follow it between detections. This was a practical way to test the idea before spending time building a labelled dataset.

The first results looked continuous, but my review showed that continuity alone was not proof of correct tracking. The detector sometimes selected a station instead of the FTS, and the tracker continued following the wrong object. I therefore stopped treating a working demonstration as sufficient evidence. I chose to focus on the FTS first, create verified ground truth, compare methods on fixed data, and keep test data separate from development decisions.

I later selected a supervised YOLO11n detector and a tracker using the measured results rather than choosing the most complicated method. I also moved the interface to FastAPI with a browser frontend because I needed the camera stream, tracking state, and controls to update independently. Once the FTS method was stable enough for the next study, I opened a separate workpiece-feasibility branch. I first checked whether red, blue, and white workpieces were actually visible in the recordings, then prepared temporal annotations before training. I kept the _2 recordings sealed so that they could remain a genuine held-out evaluation.

docs.title: Intake improvement after the meeting
docs.text: After the meeting, I returned to the first intake version that I had presented. I found that stopping the visible tracking was not enough: the MQTT intake could continue trying to reconnect and the tracking watchdog could restart work in the background. I changed the Stop tracking control so that it stops the camera and inference process, disconnects MQTT, ends the intake thread, and stays stopped until I explicitly press Start tracking. I made this choice because the operator should decide when the computer uses these resources. The validated change is recorded on branch feature/mqtt-intake-trigger in commit 1c232fe.

docs.title: Where I am now
docs.text: The detector and temporary tracker candidates are locked, and the held-out procedure was prepared before its labels were inspected. The remaining work is to complete the held-out review and describe honestly where moving-workpiece tracking is reliable and where it is still weak. From now on, I will keep the daily journal short and personal: what I did, why I chose it, what I learned, and what I will do next. Detailed metrics, commands, and configurations will remain in the experiment reports and decision register.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: I decided to preserve the evaluation of the 540 held-out frames as the baseline result for the current model. The result is provisional because I completed the annotations alone and no independent reviewer was available. For the next experiment, I will retire these frames from testing and investigate whether adding them to the development data improves a new model version.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: I could keep the 540 frames permanently as test data, use them immediately for training without preserving the current result, or adjust the current model after inspecting its held-out errors.

docs.title: Why I chose this direction
docs.text: The current model missed several frozen targets, particularly red recall and red and white tracking coverage. The annotations therefore contain useful examples of the conditions where the model is weak. Preserving the current report first keeps an honest record of the original performance. A separate training experiment also prevents the original result from being overwritten or confused with the performance of a later model.

docs.title: Implications and next steps
docs.text: Once the 540 frames are used for training, they can no longer be used to test the new model. I must record their change from held-out evidence to development data, create a separate experiment branch, and train a new model version without changing the original report. Any claim that the new model performs better will require newly recorded, unseen videos. The training data must also be balanced so that repeated static frames do not hide weaknesses during movement, station interaction, or handover.

docs.title: Why was workpiece tracking added?
docs.text: Last Friday, I met Oliver and Jonathan to review the project status. They asked me to extend the application from tracking only the FTS to also tracking the workpieces. The application should connect to the digital ORBIS SmartFactory so that an NFC-read event can start the tracking process.

docs.title: Why am I changing how I write this journal?
docs.text: On Tuesday, I showed Oliver my progress. He asked me to register my bachelor thesis quickly and keep the journal and meeting records up to date. He also said that the journal looked AI-generated and contained too much information. I therefore changed it to a shorter and more personal account of what happened, why it mattered, and what comes next.

docs.title: What did Jonathan ask me today?
docs.text: At 09:30, I met Jonathan, my university supervisor. He reminded me that I need to leave enough time to begin writing the thesis. He asked me to send him a clear overview of what is still unfinished in the project and how much time I expect each remaining task to require.

He also advised me to separate the thesis into a theoretical part and a practical part and to prepare a first table-of-contents structure. This should make the project scope and the path toward the final thesis easier to understand.

docs.text: I need a realistic plan that separates work required for the thesis from optional technical improvements. This will help me decide when to stop extending the prototype and begin writing without losing the evidence already produced. I also need to transfer this plan into Planner and connect the tasks to the first thesis outline.

I will then create the Planner structure and draft the theoretical and practical sections of the table of contents. Future journal entries will continue as short, question-led stories: what happened, why it mattered, what I learned, and what comes next.

docs.title: D-001 — Observe rather than control the shopfloor
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-13 or earlier; present in the initial project definition
  • Status: active
  • Problem: define the system boundary for a safe thesis demonstrator.
  • Decision: use cameras to observe and reconstruct Track & Trace information; never send control commands to the shopfloor.
  • Rationale: this isolates perception and interpretation, avoids operational safety risks, and permits comparison with existing system records.
  • Evidence: project instructions, README, and quality criteria.
  • Consequence: MQTT/OPC-UA may be used as evaluation reference, not as an input required for AI reconstruction.

docs.title: D-002 — Use a layered perception pipeline
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-13
  • Status: active
  • Problem: keep computer-vision and Track & Trace logic testable.
  • Decision: separate capture, detection, tracking, zone mapping, interpretation, storage, evaluation, and dashboard responsibilities.
  • Alternatives: one monolithic script or dashboard-owned processing.
  • Rationale: independent layers permit isolated tests, method replacement, and clearer experimental attribution.
  • Evidence: initial commit, package layout, README, and tests.

docs.title: D-003 — Use hybrid FTS detection and tracking for the first prototype
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-20
  • Status: active as baseline; not approved for final live transfer
  • Problem: detect an FTS without first producing a labelled training set and maintain positions between expensive detections on CPU.
  • Decision: initialize with a single-reference YOLOE visual prompt and track between periodic detections with OpenCV CSRT.
  • Alternatives: train a one-class detector immediately; use ByteTrack or BoT-SORT from the beginning; use only classical image processing.
  • Rationale: visual prompting enabled rapid zero-training prototyping, while CSRT reduced repeated inference cost and worked with one object.
  • Evidence: commit 3e47e72, hybrid scripts, and baseline configuration.
  • Limitation discovered: the detector often selected a station, after which CSRT produced a continuous but semantically wrong trajectory.

docs.title: D-004 — Replace Streamlit with FastAPI and a browser-native frontend
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-21 to 2026-07-27
  • Status: active
  • Problem: the planned Streamlit rerun model was unsuitable for direct, low-latency video and independently updating live state.
  • Decision: use FastAPI, plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, WebSocket state/events, and MJPEG annotated video.
  • Alternatives: continue Streamlit; use a React build; use a desktop GUI.
  • Rationale: the selected stack supports independent streaming channels, explicit API boundaries, a lightweight deployment, and precise frontend control without adding a frontend build system.
  • Evidence: dashboard implementation, README, dashboard tests, and current working application.

docs.title: D-005 — Use latest-frame transport for live operation
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-21 to 2026-07-27
  • Status: active
  • Problem: queued or disk-polled frames caused visible latency.
  • Decision: capture continuously, keep only the newest frame, drop stale frames, and publish the latest encoded preview through shared memory.
  • Alternatives: process every frame in order; poll image files from disk.
  • Rationale: for live observation, freshness is more important than processing every frame; stale frames make the dashboard temporally misleading.
  • Evidence: live capture and shared-preview modules plus live tests.

docs.title: D-006 — Preserve review history as append-only JSONL
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-27 to 2026-07-28
  • Status: active
  • Problem: allow human corrections without deleting experimental evidence.
  • Decision: append every verdict and treat the latest row per candidate as authoritative.
  • Alternatives: overwrite one mutable record; edit baseline outputs directly.
  • Rationale: append-only history supports traceability, correction, and reproducible summary generation.
  • Evidence: failure_review.jsonl, review service, summary generator, and regression test.

docs.title: D-007 — Evaluate the unchanged method before tuning
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-27
  • Status: active methodological rule
  • Problem: ad hoc tuning can hide failure modes and produce an irreproducible method.
  • Decision: run one recorded configuration on all six videos and review its failures before modifying thresholds or references.
  • Rationale: a fixed baseline allows later methods to be compared against the same evidence.
  • Evidence: FTS roadmap, baseline config, metrics, and review report.

docs.title: D-008 — Do not use confidence thresholding as the main correction
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-28
  • Status: active
  • Problem: determine whether a higher YOLOE confidence threshold could reject station false locks.
  • Decision: do not tune only the threshold.
  • Rationale: reviewed station false locks had a higher mean confidence (0.1354) than correct locks (0.1205); confidence therefore did not separate the classes in this baseline.
  • Evidence: manual review summary.
  • Next comparison: multi-view visual prompting versus a dedicated one-class detector on held-out videos.

docs.title: D-009 — Focus exclusively on the FTS before expanding analytics
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-28
  • Status: active
  • Problem: limit thesis scope and prevent later outputs from depending on an unreliable carrier trajectory.
  • Decision: complete FTS detection, tracking, calibration, and live validation before extending workpiece tracking, custody, event reconstruction, or detailed dashboard statistics.
  • Alternatives: develop all object classes and analytics in parallel.
  • Rationale: downstream assignments and statistics are not scientifically meaningful if the FTS itself is frequently misidentified.
  • Evidence: supervisor meeting of 2026-07-28 and FTS roadmap.

docs.title: D-010 — Seal test evidence before detector development
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-07-31
  • Status: active methodological rule
  • Problem: repeated test inspection would turn the held-out set into tuning evidence and make the final comparison optimistic.
  • Decision: permit prompt, threshold, constraint, architecture, and checkpoint selection only on train and validation sources. Keep all 26 test frames inaccessible to development runners until both detector candidates and their validation results are locked.
  • Alternatives: inspect test metrics after every change; tune all available frames; report Ultralytics defaults without a local evaluation contract.
  • Rationale: a small dataset is especially vulnerable to test leakage. A machine-enforced release gate makes the final comparison reproducible and falsifiable.
  • Evidence: configs/experiments/fts_detector_evaluation_v1.json, docs/research/FTS_DETECTOR_EVALUATION_V1.md, and evaluator regression tests.

docs.title: D-011 — Isolate workpiece feasibility from the validated FTS pipeline
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-10
  • Status: active experimental boundary
  • Problem: investigate the supervisor-proposed workpiece capability without destabilising or contaminating the selected FTS detector, tracker, Replay, Live behavior, or station-event evidence.
  • Decision: use branch experiment/workpiece-feasibility and the separate workpiece_study/ area. Read existing videos as immutable inputs; require observability, detection, tracking, and custody gates before integration.
  • Alternatives: modify the current live pipeline immediately; create an unrelated repository; acquire arbitrary new data before testing existing data.
  • Rationale: separation preserves the validated carrier evidence while allowing a falsifiable feasibility study. Existing recordings should reveal concrete visibility and coverage gaps before new acquisition is designed.
  • Scope relation: D-009 remains the application-integration boundary. This decision permits isolated feasibility preparation after FTS detector/tracker selection; it does not certify workpieces or merge them into operations.
  • Evidence: workpiece_study/PROTOCOL.md, workpiece_study/ROADMAP.md, and workpiece_study/STARTUP_RECORD.md.

docs.title: D-012 — Permit only explicit reviewed-box propagation within one recording
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-11
  • Status: active annotation rule
  • Problem: static pieces make repeated manual boxes expensive, but the 36 WP-1 frames are widely separated samples rather than consecutive video frames.
  • Decision: offer an optional copy from the closest earlier reviewed frame in the same recording. Display copied boxes as unverified, require explicit current-frame review before save, and record the source frame as provenance.
  • Rejected alternative: silently copy the first layout to every frame or propagate boxes across recordings.
  • Rationale: bounded propagation reduces repetitive work without treating a previous observation as current ground truth or hiding temporal changes.
  • Evidence: workpiece copy-source API safeguards, browser validation, and tests/test_workpiece_audit.py.

docs.title: D-013 — Advance workpiece feasibility to temporal ground truth
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-12
  • Status: active experimental decision
  • Problem: decide whether the completed WP-1 audit supports detector work, requires new acquisition, or requires stronger temporal evidence first.
  • Decision: close WP-1 as passed and begin WP-2 by freezing targeted 8–12 second sequences from the _1 development recordings. Prioritize on-FTS, station/handover, occlusion, and explicit negative conditions. Keep _2 sources sealed and defer detector comparison until the WP-2 protocol and development labels are complete.
  • Rejected alternatives: train immediately from the sparse sampled frames; open _2 sources for sequence selection; acquire new video before checking whether the existing development recordings contain the required cases.
  • Rationale: all colours and required contexts are human-observable, so immediate acquisition is not justified. However, isolated frames cannot establish temporal continuity, and the WP-1 sample contains no negatives and is dominated by static background inventory.
  • Evidence: docs/research/WORKPIECE_WP1_OBSERVABILITY.md and the completed append-only WP-1 decisions.

docs.title: D-014 — Freeze reviewed workpiece windows but reject negative hypotheses
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-14
  • Status: active experimental decision
  • Problem: decide whether the 14 proposed _1 windows are suitable for temporal annotation and whether their coarse evidence hypotheses are valid.
  • Decision: freeze all 14 original 12-second boundaries for 5 FPS annotation. Replace proposal hypotheses with the human-reviewed observations in workpiece_study/configs/temporal_candidate_review_v0.1.json.
  • Rejected alternative: treat the proposal tags as truth or discard useful station windows merely because an expected tag was incorrect.
  • Rationale: every window contains visible workpiece evidence, but the three proposed background negatives contain active DPS handling. Preserving the original proposal and recording a separate review makes the correction auditable without rewriting history.
  • Consequence: frame annotation may begin, but WP-2 cannot close until true background negatives are separately selected and verified. _2 sources remain sealed.
  • Evidence: docs/research/WORKPIECE_WP2_SEQUENCE_REVIEW.md and the checksum-bound review configuration.

docs.title: D-015 — Accept WP-2 annotation completeness without closing WP-2
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-20
  • Status: active experimental decision
  • Problem: decide whether completion of all prepared temporal-frame labels is sufficient to close WP-2 and begin detector comparison.
  • Decision: accept the development-frame annotation completeness sub-gate: 840/840 frames have authoritative decisions. Keep WP-2 open until separate background-negative evidence is selected and verified and the held-out protocol is locked.
  • Rejected alternative: treat zero pending labels as completion of the whole WP-2 milestone or reinterpret the three disproved background proposals as negatives.
  • Rationale: completeness and evidence coverage are distinct. The completed queue contains 16,835 visible instances but no absent frame, so it cannot support a defensible false-positive assessment on true background negatives.
  • Consequence: preserve the current append-only labels, keep _2 sealed, and acquire the missing negative evidence before detector comparison.
  • Evidence: docs/research/WORKPIECE_WP2_TEMPORAL_ANNOTATION.md and the evidence-bound temporal summary.

docs.title: D-016 — Accept verified spatial negatives without claiming empty frames
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-20
  • Status: active experimental decision
  • Problem: no completed temporal frame is workpiece-free, while WP-2 still requires explicit negative evidence and _2 must remain sealed.
  • Decision: accept the 30/30 human-verified 640×540 development crops as spatial negative evidence for later crop/tile false-positive analysis. Close the development ground-truth sub-gate, but explicitly keep full_frame_absence_verified = false and keep WP-2 open until the held-out annotation protocol is locked.
  • Rejected alternative: auto-label box-free proposals, reinterpret a crop as proof that its full frame is empty, open _2, or silently broaden the source policy to unrelated recordings.
  • Rationale: direct human review provides explicit negative labels within the displayed regions. All 30 candidates passed the predeclared coverage gate, while the scope statement preserves the distinction between local and whole-frame evidence.
  • Consequence: crop/tile detector experiments may use this evidence after protocol locking. Whole-frame no-object performance remains unmeasured; the 30 crops come from nine source frames and are not independent observations.
  • Evidence: docs/research/WORKPIECE_WP2_SPATIAL_NEGATIVES.md, the generated manifest, and the append-only crop decision log.

docs.title: D-017 — Lock held-out procedure and close WP-2 without opening _2
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-20
  • Status: active experimental decision
  • Problem: freeze a defensible one-time held-out evaluation before pixels can influence sampling, annotation, candidate selection, or thresholds, while avoiding a roadmap cycle between WP-2 labels and WP-3/WP-4 candidate locks.
  • Decision: lock three duration-normalized 12-second windows per _2 source, 5 FPS sampling, 540 future frames, the annotation schema, mandatory independent second review, prediction-first blinding, matching, metrics, and acceptance gates. Close WP-2 now, but do not authorize _2 release until detector and tracker candidates are both frozen and a separate release record receives explicit authorization.
  • Rejected alternative: inspect _2 to choose favorable windows, mirror development timestamps without a route correspondence, release after only a detector lock, or expose labels before raw predictions are sealed.
  • Rationale: duration-normalized metadata-only selection is reproducible and pixel-independent. Delaying release until both candidate families are locked prevents held-out temporal labels from influencing tracker development.
  • Consequence: WP-3 may begin using _1 evidence only. The future _2 result remains an internal source-held-out check, requires a different second reviewer, and cannot trigger tuning; failure requires new development work and prospective test data.
  • Evidence: workpiece_study/configs/held_out_protocol_v0.1.json and docs/research/WORKPIECE_WP2_HELD_OUT_PROTOCOL_LOCK.md.

docs.title: D-018 — Select and lock the supervised workpiece detector
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-22
  • Status: active experimental decision
  • Problem: decide whether either frozen WP-3 detector provides sufficient development evidence to begin temporary tracking without opening _2.
  • Decision: reject static-hsv-shape-v0.1 and lock supervised-yolo11n-workpiece-v0.1 for WP-4 development. Freeze checkpoint SHA-256 300f852bc6af002cc4f5897c3897aeb8391772d454b4b595c086a78b8b1c38ae, 960-pixel full-frame CPU inference, confidence 0.20, NMS IoU 0.70, and the red/blue/white class map.
  • Rationale: the supervised candidate achieved macro F1 0.9205 and recall 0.9031/0.9621/0.8917 for red/blue/white, passing the numerical gate. Review of the ten largest repeated unmatched-prediction clusters found visible workpieces/localization disagreement rather than station hardware confusers.
  • Known weakness: station-context recall is 78/144 (0.5417), with misses concentrated in red and blue manipulation/occlusion evidence. WP-4 must not hide this limitation behind aggregate accuracy.
  • Rejected alternative: promote the faster classical baseline, tune the supervised model after seeing validation errors, or open _2 before tracker lock.
  • Consequence: WP-4 may begin on _1. _2 release remains unauthorized until the tracker candidate and combined release record are locked.
  • Evidence: docs/research/WORKPIECE_WP3_DETECTOR_COMPARISON.md and workpiece_study/configs/detector_candidate_lock_v0.1.json.

docs.title: D-019 — Lock global motion association while rejecting a broad robustness claim
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-22
  • Status: active experimental decision
  • Problem: select a temporary tracker under the frozen WP-4 gate without allowing static inventory to hide material-flow failures.
  • Decision: lock global-motion-lap-association-v0.1. It uses class-aware Jonker–Volgenant assignment, constant-velocity prediction for at most 0.4 seconds, and sequence-scoped identities. Keep _2 sealed pending the separate combined release record and explicit operator confirmation.
  • Rationale: both candidates passed. The selected tracker had higher minimum per-colour coverage (0.9022 versus 0.8917), zero identity swaps, fewer ID switches (7 versus 10), and fewer fragments (30 versus 38).
  • Limitation: aggregate coverage 0.9218 is dominated by static inventory. Coverage is 0.3084 for handover, 0.3000 on-FTS, and 0.5556 at stations, with a 6.2-second longest miss. Robust moving-workpiece tracking is not claimed.
  • Rejected alternative: select the lower-latency greedy tracker contrary to the frozen ranking, tune association after validation results, or interpret the aggregate gate as production readiness.
  • Evidence: docs/research/WORKPIECE_WP4_TRACKER_COMPARISON.md and workpiece_study/configs/tracker_candidate_lock_v0.1.json.

docs.title: D-020 — Prepare the combined held-out release record without authorizing access
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-22
  • Status: active methodological checkpoint
  • Problem: bind the final detector, tracker, sampling, gates, and output schemas before _2 access without treating preparation as authorization.
  • Decision: create workpiece-held-out-release-v0.1 in prepared_pending_explicit_authorization state. Bind the held-out protocol, both candidate locks, frozen acceptance rules, and prediction-before-label ordering. Keep every sealed-access flag and permission false.
  • Rationale: a reviewable draft closes the technical reproducibility gap while preserving a separate, explicit human decision at the irreversible release boundary.
  • Remaining blockers: assign different first-pass and second reviewers and obtain explicit operator confirmation for the one-time _2 release.
  • Rejected alternative: infer authorization from the request to prepare the record, mutate candidate locks, or inspect sealed media while checking the release prerequisites.
  • Evidence: workpiece_study/configs/held_out_release_v0.1.json and docs/research/WORKPIECE_HELD_OUT_RELEASE_PREPARATION.md.

docs.title: D-021 — Authorize and seal the one-time held-out prediction streams
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-08-22
  • Status: active irreversible evaluation boundary
  • Decision: assign Daniel Wonkam as first-pass reviewer and ORIEL as the distinct independent reviewer; record explicit operator authorization; then extract only the nine frozen _2 windows and generate detector and tracker predictions before exposing images for annotation.
  • Interruption: the first attempt stopped before extraction because the codec reported 30.000125 FPS instead of metadata-rounded 30.0 FPS. Preserve that label-free failure and allow a 0.01 FPS metadata tolerance without changing any frozen frame index or analytical parameter.
  • Result: 540 frames, 540 detector rows, and 540 tracker rows were produced. Detector SHA-256 is 5c4404e22a11dd5ac7a0faab4c458096e7a2c1465fdf1bd8396e0a613c26eab0; tracker SHA-256 is caf711a7212eb2d2165e676034d299eff51a42420d57fb5e36852fa328b7b684.
  • Constraint: predictions cannot be regenerated after this boundary and cannot be exposed to either annotator. No held-out result may tune the model, threshold, sampling, crop/tile strategy, tracker, or acceptance gates.
  • Evidence: experiments/runs/20260822_workpiece_held_out_v0.1/execution_seal.json and docs/research/WORKPIECE_HELD_OUT_RELEASE_PREPARATION.md.

docs.title: D-022 — Report the held-out result as provisional without independent review
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-03
  • Status: active protocol deviation; final gate blocked
  • Problem: all 540 first-pass annotations were complete, but the assigned independent reviewer was unavailable to repeat the review.
  • Decision: record the deviation before viewing results, then evaluate the unchanged sealed predictions once against the first pass. Label every output as provisional and prevent numerical checks from becoming a final gate pass.
  • Rationale: preserving the pre-label prediction hashes still provides useful internal evidence, while an explicit limitation is more defensible than claiming independence that did not occur or discarding the completed annotation work.
  • Result: the numerical checks did not all pass. Detector macro F1 was 0.7976; red recall was 0.6667. Tracker coverage was 0.6703/0.8492/0.7222 for red/blue/white, with zero simultaneous identity swaps.
  • Constraint: do not tune against these held-out frames. If they become training data, obtain a new unseen source for later evaluation.
  • Evidence: workpiece_study/configs/held_out_single_reviewer_deviation_v0.1.json and docs/research/WORKPIECE_HELD_OUT_PROVISIONAL_EVALUATION.md.

docs.title: D-023 — Keep prospective quality review separate from annotation and scoring
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-14
  • Status: targeted QA completed 2026-09-15; scoring governed separately by D-025
  • Problem: the completed composite first pass needs a quality check without overwriting its original labels or treating completion as independent verification.
  • Decision: freeze the complete first-pass history, both seals and composite membership; structurally validate all 360 frames; prepare same-reviewer visual QA for the 60-frame replacement sequence. Preload human boxes but require explicit confirmation and reasoned corrections in a different append-only store.
  • Rationale: review of transport/handover/station transitions should not force every frame into a dual-carrier state or use detector errors as selection hints.
  • Limitations: declared after first pass, before scoring. Not independent review, not full visual QA of the other five windows, not scoring release. The earlier held-out single-reviewer deviation is not automatically transferred here.
  • Evidence: workpiece_study/configs/prospective_quality_review_v0.1.json, workpiece_study/configs/prospective_quality_review_v0.2.json, dashboard/workpiece_prospective_review.py, and the daily journals for 2026-09-14 and 2026-09-15. The final v0.2 state contains 60/60 confirmed frames, zero corrections and zero unresolved frames.

docs.title: D-024 — Recover stale QA with a new snapshot, not relaxed integrity checks
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-14 (session date)
  • Status: active; v0.2 prepared, v0.1 preserved
  • Problem: an unchanged first-pass re-save at 16:57:23 UTC extended history from 525 to 526 entries. The v0.1 byte binding correctly rejected it, but the UI misleadingly left an empty canvas, loading progress and enabled controls.
  • Decision: retain the original history and v0.1 bundle; prepare a separately configured v0.2 from current history. Do not bypass checks or transfer approvals. Disable annotation actions until the selected image is valid; expose blocked state, a specific error and a retry that never changes evidence.
  • Evidence: the old history is a byte-exact prefix of the new one and the appended record has unchanged canonical annotation fields. All other v0.1 bindings match. New configuration: workpiece_study/configs/prospective_quality_review_v0.2.json.
  • Limitation: another first-pass save still requires an explicit new version. This change neither locks the first-pass editor nor authorizes scoring.

docs.title: D-025 — Evaluate the prospective composite under a declared single-reviewer deviation
docs.text:
• Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active protocol deviation; numerical checks failed and final gate blocked
  • Problem: the 360-frame prospective first pass and targeted replacement QA were complete, but no independent reviewer was available for the next gate.
  • Decision: record Daniel Wonkam's explicit authorization before viewing results, freeze a one-time scoring release, then evaluate the unchanged sealed predictions. Keep the 300 evaluation-role frames separate from the 60 development-reserve frames and label all outputs provisional single-reviewer.
  • Bindings: the release fixes both execution seals and prediction hashes, both manifests, first-pass and QA histories, evaluation implementations, IoU 0.50, confidence 0.20, the 300/60 role split and existing numerical gates.
  • Result: on the evaluation role, detector macro F1 was 0.1193 and recall was 0.0417/0.1161/0.0580 for red/blue/white. Tracker temporal coverage was 0.0417/0.1223/0.0681, with five ID switches, zero simultaneous identity swaps and 15 fragments. Only the zero-swap numerical observation passed.
  • Development reserve: detector macro F1 was 0.2230 and tracker temporal coverage was 0.1429; these observations are reported separately and do not alter the evaluation-role decision.
  • Interpretation: the frozen candidate shows a large prospective transfer failure. The result is not a final gate pass or production certification: annotation quality lacks independent review, QA covered only the replacement sequence and station-event scoring remains unauthorized.
  • Constraint: do not tune on the evaluation-role frames. Any model, tracker, threshold or sampling change requires a new unseen prospective source before a later performance claim.
  • Evidence: workpiece_study/configs/prospective_single_reviewer_deviation_v0.1.json, workpiece_study/configs/prospective_single_reviewer_release_v0.1.json, and experiments/runs/20260915_workpiece_prospective_provisional_v0.1/PROVISIONAL_SINGLE_REVIEWER_REPORT.md.
